newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN sees weak recovery of Euro wood products in 97.
newsitem.headline: UN sees weak recovery of Euro wood products in 97.

text.p: Demand for European forest products is expected to make a weak recovery in 1997, while the market should remain satisfactory in North America due to the continuing strength of housing markets there, the Timber Committee of the U.N. Economic Commission for Europe (ECE) said.

The Geneva-based ECE, in a text issued on Thursday following a meeting last week with the Food and Agriculture Organisation's European Forestry Commission, also forecast continuation of present conditions for the transition states of eastern Europe.

"In autumn 1996, European markets for roundwood and forest products are marked, with few exceptions, by lower demand, fierce competition between products and suppliers and with non-forest products, and continuing low prices," it said.
"In North America, however, the strength of the housing market has contributed to raising consumption levels in satisfactory market conditions," it added.

The forest products sector of the countries in transition in eastern Europe was now recovering from the deep recession of the early 1990s, but differences between national situations were becoming ever more marked, according to the ECE text.
"Production in Russia continues to fall, but more slowly than in previous years."

The text concluded: "For 1997, a weak recovery in demand for forest products is expected for Europe, and a continuation of present market conditions for North America and the countries in transition."

Construction activity in Europe is expected to drop by three percent in 1996, with a slight recovery overall in 1997, but marked by a further drop of 2.1 percent in new residential construction, according to ECE, citing statistics by Euroconstruct, an association of European trade institutions.
In the United States, new housing construction remained at a relatively high rate through much of the year, the ECE said.
"If mortgage rates are not raised, housing starts may total 1.45 million in 1996 and 1.4 million if rates are raised."
